Functions of a Complex Variable

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • test complex differentiability using the Cauchy--Riemann equations;

  • apply Cauchy’s theorem and integral formula with their domain hypotheses;

  • classify isolated singularities from a Laurent series; and

  • compute contour and real-line integrals using residues.

Complex Numbers¶

A complex number is

z=x+iy,x,y∈R.z = x + i y, \qquad x, y \in \mathbb{R}.z=x+iy,x,y∈R.
(1)

We consider functions

f:C→C.f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}.f:C→C.
(2)

We can always rewrite any complex function as

f(z)=u(x,y)+i v(x,y),f(z) = u(x,y) + i\, v(x,y),f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y),
(3)

where u,vu,vu,v are real-valued functions.

Complex Differentiability¶

The derivative of a complex function is

f′(z0)=lim⁡z→z0f(z)−f(z0)z−z0.f'(z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{f(z) - f(z_0)}{z - z_0}.f′(z0​)=z→z0​lim​z−z0​f(z)−f(z0​)​.
(4)

What the original figure plots. It shows several paths approaching the same point in the complex plane.

What this is trying to convey. Complex differentiability requires the difference quotient to approach one value along every possible path to the point.

Polished version.

Key idea:

  • In R\mathbb{R}R, there is only one direction to approach.

  • In C\mathbb{C}C, zzz can approach through infinitely many paths.

Therefore the quotient must have the same limit along every path, not merely along straight-line directions.

Holomorphic Functions¶

Note

Definition A function is holomorphic (or analytic or regular or monogenic) in a domain if it is complex differentiable at every point there.

Note

Note The statement “f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic at a point z=az = az=a” means that f(z)f(z)f(z) has a derivative at every point inside some small circle about z=az = az=a.

Holomorphic functions are extremely well-behaved:

  • infinitely differentiable

  • equal to their Taylor series

  • integrals over closed loops vanish when the loop can be contracted within the holomorphic domain

  • uniquely determined on a connected domain by values on any subset having an accumulation point in that domain

Cauchy--Riemann Equations¶

Note

Theorem

If f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y) is analytic in a region, then in that region:

ux=vy,uy=−vx.\boxed{ \begin{aligned} u_x &= v_y,\\ u_y &= -v_x. \end{aligned}}ux​uy​​=vy​,=−vx​.​​
(5)

These are the [Cauchy--Riemann (CR) conditions]{style=“color: blue”}.

Note

Theorem If CR holds, and u(x,y)u(x,y)u(x,y) and v(x,y)v(x,y)v(x,y) and their partial derivatives are continuous in a region, then f(z)f(z)f(z) is complex differentiable (holomorphic) in the region.

Example: f(z)=z2f(z) = z^2f(z)=z2¶

Let z=x+iyz = x + iyz=x+iy.

z2=(x2−y2)+i(2xy).z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy).z2=(x2−y2)+i(2xy).
(6)

Thus

u=x2−y2,v=2xy.u = x^2 - y^2, \qquad v = 2xy.u=x2−y2,v=2xy.
(7)

Compute:

ux=2x=vy,uy=−2y=−vx.u_x = 2x = v_y, \qquad u_y = -2y = -v_x.ux​=2x=vy​,uy​=−2y=−vx​.
(8)

CR hold everywhere ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ fff is holomorphic on C\mathbb{C}C.

Examples of Holomorphic Functions¶

Entire functions (holomorphic on all of C\mathbb{C}C):

  • polynomials

  • eze^zez

  • sin⁡z,cos⁡z\sin z, \cos zsinz,cosz

  • power series with infinite radius of convergence

Meromorphic functions (holomorphic except poles):

  • rational functions

  • 1/z1/z1/z (pole at 0)

Branch‐cut functions:

  • log⁡z\log zlogz, zαz^\alphazα, z\sqrt{z}z​

Singularities¶

Note

Definition A regular point of f(z)f(z)f(z) is a point at which f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic.

Note

Definition A singular point or singularity of f(z)f(z)f(z) is a point at which f(z)f(z)f(z) is not analytic.

It is called an isolated singular point if f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic everywhere else inside some small circle about the singular point.

Types of singularities:

  • Removable: sin⁡zz\frac{\sin z}{z}zsinz​ at z=0z=0z=0

  • Poles: (z−1)−3(z-1)^{-3}(z−1)−3

  • Essential: e1/ze^{1/z}e1/z at z=0z=0z=0 (wild behavior)

Understanding singularities is key to evaluating integrals using residues.

Contour Integrals¶

A [contour integral]{style=“color: blue”} along a path γ\gammaγ:

∮γf(z) dz.\oint_\gamma f(z)\, dz.∮γ​f(z)dz.
(9)

Cauchy’s Theorem:

If fff is holomorphic on and inside a closed contour CCC, then

∮Cf(z) dz=0.\oint_C f(z)\, dz = 0.∮C​f(z)dz=0.
(10)

Key idea: The integral vanishes because fff is holomorphic throughout the region bounded by the contour. If the domain has holes or excluded singularities, a closed-loop integral need not vanish.

Consequences:

  • All closed-path integrals of analytic functions vanish.

  • Contours may be continuously deformed without changing the integral.

  • Cauchy integral formula follows immediately.

Example 1: Integral of a Polynomial Over a Closed Contour¶

Evaluate

∮Γ(3z2−4z+7) dz,\oint_{\Gamma} (3z^2 - 4z + 7)\, dz,∮Γ​(3z2−4z+7)dz,
(11)

where Γ\GammaΓ is any simple closed loop in C\mathbb{C}C.

Reasoning:

  • Polynomials are analytic everywhere.

  • Cauchy’s theorem applies directly.

∮Γ(3z2−4z+7) dz=0.\boxed{\displaystyle \oint_{\Gamma} (3z^2 - 4z + 7)\, dz = 0.}∮Γ​(3z2−4z+7)dz=0.​
(12)

Example 2: Path Deformation¶

Compute

∫Γ1ezz−1 dz,\int_{\Gamma_1} \frac{e^z}{z-1}\, dz,∫Γ1​​z−1ez​dz,
(13)

where Γ1\Gamma_1Γ1​ encloses no singularity of the integrand.

Observation:

ezz−1\frac{e^z}{z-1}z−1ez​
(14)

is analytic everywhere inside Γ1\Gamma_1Γ1​ except at z=1z=1z=1. But if 1 is outside Γ1\Gamma_1Γ1​, Cauchy’s theorem implies:

∫Γ1ezz−1 dz=0.\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{\Gamma_1} \frac{e^z}{z-1}\, dz = 0. }∫Γ1​​z−1ez​dz=0.​
(15)

Idea: Contour can be shrunk to a point without crossing the singularity.

Example 3: Different Contours Give the Same Result¶

Let Γ1\Gamma_1Γ1​ and Γ2\Gamma_2Γ2​ be two contours enclosing the same region where f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic.

∫Γ1cos⁡(z) dz=∫Γ2cos⁡(z) dz.\int_{\Gamma_1} \cos(z)\, dz = \int_{\Gamma_2} \cos(z)\, dz.∫Γ1​​cos(z)dz=∫Γ2​​cos(z)dz.
(16)

Reason:

∮Γ1−Γ2cos⁡(z) dz=0⇒∫Γ1cos⁡(z) dz=∫Γ2cos⁡(z) dz.\oint_{\Gamma_1 - \Gamma_2} \cos(z)\, dz = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \int_{\Gamma_1} \cos(z)\, dz = \int_{\Gamma_2} \cos(z)\, dz.∮Γ1​−Γ2​​cos(z)dz=0⇒∫Γ1​​cos(z)dz=∫Γ2​​cos(z)dz.
(17)

Example: A circle, a triangle, or a square around no singularities give identical results (all zero).

Example 4: Shrinking a Contour Around an Isolated Singularity¶

Consider

∫Γ1z dz,\int_{\Gamma} \frac{1}{z}\, dz,∫Γ​z1​dz,
(18)

where Γ\GammaΓ is any simple loop wrapping once around z=0z=0z=0.

Even though f(z)=1/zf(z)=1/zf(z)=1/z is not analytic at the origin, the contour can be deformed to any other closed path linking the origin.

∫Γ1z dz=∫∣z∣=ε1z dz=∫02πi dθ=2πi.\int_{\Gamma} \frac{1}{z}\, dz = \int_{|z|=\varepsilon} \frac{1}{z}\, dz = \int_0^{2\pi} i\, d\theta = 2\pi i.∫Γ​z1​dz=∫∣z∣=ε​z1​dz=∫02π​idθ=2πi.
(19)

Here we used z=εeiθz = \varepsilon e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=εeiθ, dz=iεeiθdθdz = \mathrm{i}\varepsilon e^{i\theta}d\thetadz=iεeiθdθ

Key point: Contour deformations are valid as long as the singularity is not crossed.

Example 5: Using Cauchy’s Theorem to Avoid a Hard Integral¶

Evaluate

∫Γz5sin⁡(z) dz,\int_{\Gamma} z^5 \sin(z)\, dz,∫Γ​z5sin(z)dz,
(20)

where Γ\GammaΓ is an ellipse enclosing no singularities of the integrand.

Observation: z5sin⁡(z)z^5\sin(z)z5sin(z) is entire (analytic everywhere).

∫Γz5sin⁡(z) dz=0.\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{\Gamma} z^5 \sin(z)\, dz = 0.}∫Γ​z5sin(z)dz=0.​
(21)

This avoids computing a messy antiderivative!

Cauchy Integral Formula¶

If f(z)f(z)f(z) is holomorphic inside and on a simple closed contour CCC, the value of f(z)f(z)f(z) at a point z=az = az=a inside CCC is given by the following contour integral along CCC:

f(z0)=12πi∮Cf(z)z−z0 dz.\boxed{ f(z_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{C} \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\, dz. }f(z0​)=2πi1​∮C​z−z0​f(z)​dz.​
(22)

Interpretation:

  • An analytic function is completely determined by its boundary values.

  • The integrand has a simple pole at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​.

  • The integral extracts the value of fff at z0z_0z0​.

Geometric intuition: The contour “samples” f(z)f(z)f(z) around z0z_0z0​ and reconstructs the value at the center.

Example: Using Cauchy’s Integral Formula¶

Evaluate

∮Γezz−2 dz,\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{e^{z}}{z - 2}\, dz,∮Γ​z−2ez​dz,
(23)

where Γ\GammaΓ is any contour enclosing z=2z=2z=2.

Apply the formula:

∮Γf(z)z−z0 dz=2πi f(z0).\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\, dz = 2\pi i\, f(z_0).∮Γ​z−z0​f(z)​dz=2πif(z0​).
(24)

Here f(z)=ezf(z) = e^{z}f(z)=ez and z0=2z_0 = 2z0​=2:

∮Γezz−2 dz=2πi e2.\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{e^{z}}{z - 2}\, dz = 2\pi i\, e^{2}.∮Γ​z−2ez​dz=2πie2.
(25)

No need to evaluate by parametrizing the contour!

Cauchy’s Integral Formula for Derivatives¶

For n≥1n \ge 1n≥1,

f(n)(z0)=n!2πi∮Γf(z)(z−z0) n+1 dz.f^{(n)}(z_0) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{\,n+1}}\, dz.f(n)(z0​)=2πin!​∮Γ​(z−z0​)n+1f(z)​dz.
(26)

Example:

∮Γcos⁡z(z−1)3 dz=2πi⋅12!cos⁡′′(1).\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{\cos z}{(z - 1)^3}\, dz = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2!} \cos''(1).∮Γ​(z−1)3cosz​dz=2πi⋅2!1​cos′′(1).
(27)

Usefulness:

  • Computes derivatives without differentiating.

  • Key tool for evaluating integrals with higher-order poles.

Example: Integrating Around a Simple Pole¶

Evaluate

∮Γz2+1z−i dz,\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{z^2 + 1}{z - i}\, dz,∮Γ​z−iz2+1​dz,
(28)

where Γ\GammaΓ encloses z=iz=iz=i once.

Identify:

f(z)=g(z)z−i,g(z)=z2+1.f(z) = \frac{g(z)}{z-i}, \qquad g(z) = z^2 + 1.f(z)=z−ig(z)​,g(z)=z2+1.
(29)
∮Γf(z) dz=2πi g(i)=2πi (i2+1)=2πi(−1+1)=0.\oint_{\Gamma} f(z)\, dz = 2\pi i\, g(i) = 2\pi i\, (i^2 + 1) = 2\pi i( -1 + 1 ) = 0.∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πig(i)=2πi(i2+1)=2πi(−1+1)=0.
(30)

Here g(i)=0g(i)=0g(i)=0, so the apparent singularity is removable: (z2+1)/(z−i)=z+i(z^2+1)/(z-i)=z+i(z2+1)/(z−i)=z+i for z≠iz\ne iz=i. The contour integral vanishes because the integrand extends holomorphically through z=iz=iz=i.

Example: Contour Enclosing Several Poles¶

Evaluate

∮Γ(1z−1+2z+2)dz,\oint_{\Gamma} \left( \frac{1}{z-1} + \frac{2}{z+2} \right) dz,∮Γ​(z−11​+z+22​)dz,
(31)

where Γ\GammaΓ encloses both z=1z=1z=1 and z=−2z=-2z=−2.

∮Γ1z−1dz=2πi,∮Γ2z+2dz=2πi⋅2.\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{1}{z-1} dz = 2\pi i, \qquad \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{2}{z+2} dz = 2\pi i \cdot 2.∮Γ​z−11​dz=2πi,∮Γ​z+22​dz=2πi⋅2.
(32)
∮Γ(1z−1+2z+2)dz=2πi(1+2)=6πi.\boxed{ \oint_{\Gamma} \left(\frac{1}{z-1}+\frac{2}{z+2}\right)dz =2\pi i(1+2)=6\pi i. }∮Γ​(z−11​+z+22​)dz=2πi(1+2)=6πi.​
(33)

Each pole contributes independently.

Laurent Series: Definition¶

Let f(z)f(z)f(z) be analytic on an annulus

A={z:r<∣z−z0∣<R}.A = \{ z : r < |z - z_0| < R \}.A={z:r<∣z−z0​∣<R}.
(34)

Then f(z)f(z)f(z) can be expanded in series convergent in AAA:

f(z)=∑n=−∞∞an(z−z0)n,f(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a_n (z - z_0)^n,f(z)=n=−∞∑∞​an​(z−z0​)n,
(35)

where the coefficients are given by

an=12πi∮∣z−z0∣=ρf(z)(z−z0) n+1 dz,r<ρ<R.a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-z_0|=\rho} \frac{f(z)}{(z-z_0)^{\,n+1}}\, dz, \qquad r < \rho < R.an​=2πi1​∮∣z−z0​∣=ρ​(z−z0​)n+1f(z)​dz,r<ρ<R.
(36)

This is a [Laurent series]{style=“color: blue”}.

Structure:

  • Positive-power terms: regular (analytic) part

  • Negative-power terms: principal part

Annulus in the Complex Plane¶

Definition

An annulus in the complex plane is the set

A={ z∈C:R1<∣z−z0∣<R2 },A = \{\, z \in \mathbb{C} : R_1 < |z - z_0| < R_2 \,\},A={z∈C:R1​<∣z−z0​∣<R2​},
(37)

where z0z_0z0​ is the center and 0≤R1<R20 \le R_1 < R_20≤R1​<R2​.

  • It is the region between two concentric circles.

  • Laurent series converge on an annulus, not on a disk.

  • Different singularities inside the inner circle determine the negative-power terms.

  • Analyticity in the region outside the inner radius ensures convergence there.

Classifying Singularities via Laurent Series¶

The Laurent series determines the nature of an isolated singularity at z0z_0z0​:

  • Removable singularity: All negative-power coefficients vanish:

a−1=a−2=⋯=0.a_{-1} = a_{-2} = \cdots = 0.a−1​=a−2​=⋯=0.
(38)

  • Pole of order mmm:

a−m≠0,but a−(m+1)=a−(m+2)=⋯=0.a_{-m} \neq 0,\quad\text{but } a_{-(m+1)} = a_{-(m+2)} = \cdots = 0.a−m​=0,but a−(m+1)​=a−(m+2)​=⋯=0.
(39)

  • Essential singularity: Infinitely many negative-power terms:

a−1,a−2,… not eventually zero.a_{-1}, a_{-2}, \dots \text{ not eventually zero}.a−1​,a−2​,… not eventually zero.
(40)

Key idea: The principal part encodes the singular behavior.

Laurent Expansion: Example¶

Consider

f(z)=11−z.f(z)=\frac{1}{1-z}.f(z)=1−z1​.
(41)

Case 1: If ∣z∣<1|z|<1∣z∣<1, use the geometric series:

11−z=∑n=0∞zn.\frac{1}{1-z} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^n.1−z1​=n=0∑∞​zn.
(42)

This is a Taylor series (no negative powers). It converges in the disk ∣z∣<1|z|<1∣z∣<1.

Laurent Expansion for ∣z∣>1|z|>1∣z∣>1¶

Rewrite the function:

11−z=−1z11−1z.\frac{1}{1-z} = -\frac{1}{z}\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{z}}.1−z1​=−z1​1−z1​1​.
(43)

Now expand the geometric series in 1z\frac{1}{z}z1​:

−1z∑n=0∞(1z)n=−∑n=1∞z−n.-\frac{1}{z} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{z}\right)^n = -\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} z^{-n}.−z1​n=0∑∞​(z1​)n=−n=1∑∞​z−n.
(44)

This is a Laurent series with only negative powers. It converges in the annulus:

∣z∣>1.|z|>1.∣z∣>1.
(45)

Why Two Different Series?¶

The function f(z)=11−zf(z)=\frac{1}{1-z}f(z)=1−z1​ has a singularity at z=1z=1z=1.

  • Expansion around z=0z=0z=0 depends on distance to the singularity.

  • If ∣z∣<1|z|<1∣z∣<1: the singularity is outside, so a Taylor series converges.

  • If ∣z∣>1|z|>1∣z∣>1: the singularity is inside the contour, requiring negative powers.

Thus the Laurent series converges in two separate regions:

{Disk ∣z∣<1:∑n=0∞zn,Exterior ∣z∣>1:−∑n=1∞z−n.\begin{cases} \text{Disk } |z|<1: & \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty z^n,\\[6pt] \text{Exterior } |z|>1: & \displaystyle -\sum_{n=1}^\infty z^{-n}. \end{cases}⎩⎨⎧​Disk ∣z∣<1:Exterior ∣z∣>1:​n=0∑∞​zn,−n=1∑∞​z−n.​
(46)

Laurent Series: Example¶

Note

Example Write Laurent Series of 1z(1−z)\frac{1}{z(1-z)}z(1−z)1​

We expand

1z(1−z)=1z⋅11−z\frac{1}{z(1-z)} = \frac{1}{z} \cdot \frac{1}{1-z}z(1−z)1​=z1​⋅1−z1​
(47)

For ∣z∣<1|z|<1∣z∣<1:

11−z=∑n=0∞zn.\frac{1}{1-z} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^n.1−z1​=n=0∑∞​zn.
(48)

Thus

1z(1−z)=∑n=0∞zn−1=z−1+1+z+z2+⋯\frac{1}{z(1-z)} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^{n-1} = z^{-1} + 1 + z + z^2 + \cdotsz(1−z)1​=n=0∑∞​zn−1=z−1+1+z+z2+⋯
(49)

Principal part: z−1z^{-1}z−1
Regular part: 1+z+z2+⋯1 + z + z^2 + \cdots1+z+z2+⋯

Residue of a Function at a Pole¶

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has an isolated singularity at z0z_0z0​ with Laurent expansion

f(z)=⋯+a−1z−z0+a0+a1(z−z0)+⋯ ,f(z) = \cdots + \frac{a_{-1}}{z - z_0} + a_0 + a_1 (z - z_0) + \cdots,f(z)=⋯+z−z0​a−1​​+a0​+a1​(z−z0​)+⋯,
(50)

then the residue of f(z)f(z)f(z) at z0z_0z0​ is

Res⁡(f,z0)=a−1.\operatorname{Res}(f, z_0) = a_{-1}.Res(f,z0​)=a−1​.
(51)

Interpretation: The residue is the coefficient of the (z−z0)−1(z - z_0)^{-1}(z−z0​)−1 term in the Laurent series.

Residue Theorem¶

Let f(z)f(z)f(z) be analytic in a domain except for isolated singularities z1,…,znz_1,\dots,z_nz1​,…,zn​ inside a positively oriented contour Γ\GammaΓ.

Then the [Residue Theorem]{style=“color: blue”} is valid:

∮Γf(z) dz=2πi∑k=1nRes⁡(f,zk).\oint_{\Gamma} f(z)\, dz = 2\pi i \sum_{k=1}^{n} \operatorname{Res}(f, z_k).∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πik=1∑n​Res(f,zk​).
(52)

Consequences:

  • Integral depends only on the residues inside Γ\GammaΓ.

  • Contour shape does not matter (homotopy invariance).

  • Reduces contour integrals to local expansions at singularities.

Computing Residues of Rational Functions¶

Residue at a Simple Pole

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has a simple pole at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​, then

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=lim⁡z→z0(z−z0)f(z).\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0} f(z) = \lim_{z\to z_0} (z - z_0) f(z).Resz=z0​​f(z)=z→z0​lim​(z−z0​)f(z).
(53)

Example:

f(z)=1z(z−1)f(z) = \frac{1}{z(z-1)}f(z)=z(z−1)1​
(54)

has simple poles at z=0z=0z=0 and z=1z=1z=1.

Res⁡z=0f(z)=lim⁡z→0z 1z(z−1)=−1.\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} f(z) = \lim_{z\to 0} z\,\frac{1}{z(z-1)} = -1.Resz=0​f(z)=z→0lim​zz(z−1)1​=−1.
(55)
Res⁡z=1f(z)=lim⁡z→1(z−1)1z(z−1)=11=1.\operatorname{Res}_{z=1} f(z) = \lim_{z\to 1} (z-1)\frac{1}{z(z-1)} = \frac{1}{1} = 1.Resz=1​f(z)=z→1lim​(z−1)z(z−1)1​=11​=1.
(56)

Residues at Higher-Order Poles¶

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has a pole of order mmm at z0z_0z0​, then

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=1(m−1)!lim⁡z→z0d m−1dz m−1[(z−z0)mf(z)].\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0}f(z) = \frac{1}{(m-1)!} \lim_{z\to z_0} \frac{d^{\,m-1}}{dz^{\,m-1}} \left[(z - z_0)^m f(z)\right].Resz=z0​​f(z)=(m−1)!1​z→z0​lim​dzm−1dm−1​[(z−z0​)mf(z)].
(57)

Special case: Pole of order 2

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=lim⁡z→z0ddz[(z−z0)2f(z)].\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0}f(z) = \lim_{z\to z_0} \frac{d}{dz}\left[(z - z_0)^2 f(z)\right].Resz=z0​​f(z)=z→z0​lim​dzd​[(z−z0​)2f(z)].
(58)

Using Residues to Evaluate Real Integrals¶

Goal: Compute integrals of the form

∫−∞∞g(x) dx.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,dx.∫−∞∞​g(x)dx.
(59)

Method:

  1. Extend g(x)g(x)g(x) to a complex function f(z)f(z)f(z).

  2. Integrate f(z)f(z)f(z) around a contour that contains the real axis.

  3. Use Cauchy’s Residue Theorem:

∮f(z) dz=2πi∑Res⁡f(z).\oint f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i \sum \operatorname{Res} f(z).∮f(z)dz=2πi∑Resf(z).
(60)

  1. Show the integral on the large semicircle vanishes.

  2. If the chosen contour is positively oriented and contains no real-axis poles, conclude

∫−∞∞g(x) dx=2πi∑Res⁡f(z).\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,dx = 2\pi i\sum \operatorname{Res} f(z).∫−∞∞​g(x)dx=2πi∑Resf(z).
(61)

Example: A Standard Residue Calculation¶

Evaluate:

I=∫−∞∞dxx2+1.I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}.I=∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​.
(62)

Complex extension:

f(z)=1z2+1=1(z−i)(z+i).f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 + 1} = \frac{1}{(z-i)(z+i)}.f(z)=z2+11​=(z−i)(z+i)1​.
(63)

Pole inside upper semicircle: z=iz=iz=i.

Res⁡z=if(z)=lim⁡z→i(z−i)1(z−i)(z+i)=12i.\operatorname{Res}_{z=i} f(z) = \lim_{z\to i} (z-i) \frac{1}{(z-i)(z+i)} = \frac{1}{2i}.Resz=i​f(z)=z→ilim​(z−i)(z−i)(z+i)1​=2i1​.
(64)

Thus the contour integral equals:

2πi⋅12i=π.2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2i} = \pi.2πi⋅2i1​=π.
(65)

Semicircle contribution →0\to 0→0, so:

∫−∞∞dxx2+1=π.\boxed{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2+1} = \pi }.∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​=π​.
(66)

Semicircle Contribution Vanishes¶

Parameterize semicircle: z=Reiθ,θ∈[0,π]z = R e^{i\theta}, \theta \in [0, \pi]z=Reiθ,θ∈[0,π], dz=iReiθdθdz = i R e^{i\theta} d\thetadz=iReiθdθ.

∫semicircledzz2+1=∫0πiReiθdθR2e2iθ+1\int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} = \int_0^\pi \frac{i R e^{i\theta} d\theta}{R^2 e^{2i\theta} + 1}∫semicircle​z2+1dz​=∫0π​R2e2iθ+1iReiθdθ​
(67)

Estimate magnitude:

∣∫semicircledzz2+1∣≤∫0πR dθR2−1=πRR2−1⟶0(R→∞).\left| \int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} \right| \leq\int_0^\pi\frac{R\,d\theta}{R^2-1} =\frac{\pi R}{R^2-1} \longrightarrow0 \qquad(R\to\infty).∣∣​∫semicircle​z2+1dz​∣∣​≤∫0π​R2−1Rdθ​=R2−1πR​⟶0(R→∞).
(68)

Conclusion: Semicircle does not contribute in the limit R→∞R \to \inftyR→∞.

Real-Line Integral vs Semicircle Contribution¶

Consider the integral

∫−∞∞dxx2+1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​
(69)

computed using a semicircular contour in the upper half-plane.

Contour:

  • Real axis: −R→R-R \to R−R→R (horizontal)

  • Semicircle of radius RRR in the upper half-plane

Decomposition:

∮Cdzz2+1=∫−RRdxx2+1⏟Real-line integral (non-zero)+∫semicircledzz2+1⏟Semicircle integral (vanishes as R→∞)\oint_C \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} = \underbrace{\int_{-R}^{R} \frac{dx}{x^2+1}}_{\text{Real-line integral (non-zero)}} + \underbrace{\int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1}}_{\text{Semicircle integral (vanishes as $R\to\infty$)}}∮C​z2+1dz​=Real-line integral (non-zero)∫−RR​x2+1dx​​​+Semicircle integral (vanishes as R→∞)∫semicircle​z2+1dz​​​
(70)

Real-Line Integral vs Semicircle Contribution - cont¶

Key points:

  • The integrand along the real axis is positive and decays as 1/x21/x^21/x2 for large ∣x∣|x|∣x∣, so the integral is finite and non-zero.

  • The semicircle integral vanishes in the limit R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ because ∣f(z)∣∼1/R2|f(z)| \sim 1/R^2∣f(z)∣∼1/R2 for large ∣z∣|z|∣z∣.

  • Using the Residue Theorem:

∫−∞∞dxx2+1=2πi⋅Res⁡(1z2+1,i)=π\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2+1} = 2\pi i \cdot \operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{1}{z^2+1}, i\right) = \pi∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​=2πi⋅Res(z2+11​,i)=π
(71)

Conclusion: Only the real-line integral contributes to the final value; the semicircle “disappears.”

Example: Evaluate a Contour Integral Using Residues¶

Compute

∮Γzz2+1 dz\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{z}{z^2 + 1} \, dz∮Γ​z2+1z​dz
(72)

where Γ\GammaΓ encloses z=iz=iz=i and z=−iz=-iz=−i.

Poles:

z=i,z=−i.z = i, \quad z = -i.z=i,z=−i.
(73)

Residues:

Res⁡(f,i)=i2i=12,Res⁡(f,−i)=−i−2i=12.\operatorname{Res}(f,i) = \frac{i}{2i} = \frac12, \qquad \operatorname{Res}(f,-i) = \frac{-i}{-2i} = \frac12.Res(f,i)=2ii​=21​,Res(f,−i)=−2i−i​=21​.
(74)

Thus

∮Γzz2+1dz=2πi(12+12)=2πi.\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{z}{z^2+1}dz = 2\pi i \left(\frac12 + \frac12\right) = 2\pi i.∮Γ​z2+1z​dz=2πi(21​+21​)=2πi.
(75)

Example: Higher Order Pole¶

Evaluate

∫−∞∞x2(x2+4)2 dx.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{(x^2+4)^2}\, dx.∫−∞∞​(x2+4)2x2​dx.
(76)

Complex extension:

f(z)=z2(z2+4)2=z2(z−2i)2(z+2i)2.f(z)=\frac{z^2}{(z^2+4)^2} =\frac{z^2}{(z-2i)^2(z+2i)^2}.f(z)=(z2+4)2z2​=(z−2i)2(z+2i)2z2​.
(77)

Upper half-plane pole: z=2iz=2iz=2i (order 2).

Res⁡z=2if(z)=11!lim⁡z→2iddz[(z−2i)2f(z)].\operatorname{Res}_{z=2i} f(z) = \frac{1}{1!}\lim_{z\to 2i} \frac{d}{dz}\left[(z-2i)^2 f(z)\right].Resz=2i​f(z)=1!1​z→2ilim​dzd​[(z−2i)2f(z)].
(78)

Compute derivative...

Final result:

∫−∞∞x2(x2+4)2 dx=π4.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{(x^2+4)^2}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{4}.∫−∞∞​(x2+4)2x2​dx=4π​.
(79)
